editorial_policy.verified_means: The cited work-level claims in this profile were checked against the listed sources. It does not mean every interpretation is a source fact, every content warning is exhaustive, or the reader’s exact edition has been identified.
editorial_policy.edition_policy: Edition-specific page counts and audio durations remain examples unless the reader’s exact ISBN/format matches. Do not copy them into the protected catalog as universal values.

profiles.title: The Wee Free Men
profiles.author: Terry Pratchett
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level synopsis, Tiffany Aching placement and first-publication date verified from the author’s official site. No exact reader edition, cover or audiobook format has been identified.

publication.basis: Terry Pratchett official book page gives 1 May 2003.

profiles.genre_and_form: Comic fantasy with a young protagonist; the official author site places it in the Tiffany Aching novels within Discworld. The profile treats the story as both a fairy-tale quest and a coming-of-age narrative; that second description is editorial interpretation.

series.name: Tiffany Aching / Discworld
series.sequence_status: Official Tiffany Aching collection/category supports the five-book sequence; the 2027 plan includes the first two in this cohort.

profiles.summary: Nine-year-old Tiffany Aching lives on the Chalk, where her late grandmother’s reputation as a shepherdess and possible witch still shapes how Tiffany understands the land. Strange incursions from Fairyland unsettle the ordinary world around her. When her younger brother disappears, Tiffany joins forces with the Nac Mac Feegle—the tiny, combative pictsies known as the Wee Free Men—and sets out to bring him home. The setup is deliberately folkloric, but Tiffany’s most important equipment is not a grand destiny or a magical weapon: it is observation, stubbornness and practical judgment.
profiles.author_and_work_background: The official chronology dates the novel to 1 May 2003 and records it as the thirtieth Discworld book. The same chronology records the 2004 Locus Award for Best Young Adult Book for this title. The official Tiffany Aching page follows Tiffany across five books, allowing this novel to be read as the opening of a sustained character arc rather than an isolated Discworld side trip.
profiles.before_reading: The story uses the vocabulary and comic logic of Pratchett’s Discworld, but its central viewpoint is a child encountering a frightening and unfamiliar world. Knowing Discworld lore is not presented by the official series materials as a prerequisite. The author’s official synopsis gives the Chalk and Granny Aching particular importance, so notice how place, work and inherited memory influence Tiffany before the quest begins.
profiles.literary_approach: The book sets a grounded rural landscape against exaggerated fairy-tale danger. Its humor does not simply cancel fear; it lets the narrative examine fear without surrendering to it. The Feegles’ exaggerated speech and behavior create comic disruption, while Tiffany’s careful attention provides a steadier counterweight. Reading this as a story about practical intelligence is an interpretation, not a publisher-stated single meaning.
profiles.context: The author’s official material identifies the Chalk, shepherding and Granny Aching as central elements. The novel’s use of witches and fairy-tale creatures belongs to fantasy tradition, but the particular social rules of the Chalk are invented for the story. Avoid treating the fictional culture as a documentary account of rural British history.

themes.label: Care as competence
themes.discussion: Tiffany’s willingness to notice what others overlook suggests that care can be active, skilled work rather than sentiment alone.

themes.label: Inheritance without imitation
themes.discussion: Granny Aching matters to Tiffany, but the younger character must decide what to carry forward in her own way.

themes.label: Courage and practical reason
themes.discussion: The quest invites a comparison between heroic appearance and the quieter work of assessing a situation accurately.

themes.label: Community across difference
themes.discussion: Tiffany and the Feegles cooperate despite their very different habits and assumptions.

profiles.personal_fit: This is a strong pathway match if you enjoy nature and place-based fantasy, a capable young heroine, folklore, and humor that has something serious underneath it. It also offers a useful literary counterpoint for thinking about care, responsibility and inherited identity without turning those ideas into a lecture.
profiles.possible_mismatch: The voice is comic and deliberately unruly. Readers seeking solemn, court-centered epic fantasy may find the Feegles’ antics intentionally chaotic. Its protagonist is nine, so the narrative’s emotional and practical scale is often child-centered even when the themes reach beyond childhood.

notes: The official synopsis includes a missing younger child, threatening fairy-tale creatures and peril during a rescue quest.
Granny Aching is already dead when the story begins; bereavement is part of the setup.
This is not an exhaustive content-warning audit.

reading_questions: What does Tiffany notice that the adults around her overlook?
How does the Chalk function as more than a backdrop?
When does common sense become a form of courage?
discussion_questions: Does the novel treat inherited wisdom as something to preserve, revise, or both?
How does Pratchett use comic exaggeration to make danger readable without making it meaningless?

related_connections.label: Next in Tiffany Aching sequence
related_connections.note: A Hat Full of Sky continues Tiffany’s story at a later age; the author’s official pages identify it as the next Tiffany novel.

profiles.title: Think
profiles.author: Simon Blackburn
profiles.verification_scope: Title-level contents and 1999 Oxford University Press bibliographic records checked. The exact edition intended by the reader is not known; page counts differ across records.

publication.basis: Google Books and Open Library records identify Oxford University Press, 1999.

profiles.genre_and_form: Introductory philosophy written for general readers. The contents are organized into eight broad chapters: knowledge, mind, free will, the self, God, reasoning, the world and what to do.

series.sequence_status: Standalone introduction; no series placement identified.

profiles.summary: Think begins with questions that can feel both ordinary and unsettling: how can we know the world is real, what is a mind, are we free, what makes a self persist, and how should we reason about God, truth and value? Simon Blackburn uses these problems to introduce philosophical argument rather than treating philosophy as a list of famous names. The chapter structure moves from knowledge and mind through freedom, identity, religious argument, reasoning and the world, before turning toward practical questions. It is an invitation to examine the assumptions that make everyday thinking possible.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Google Books and Open Library identify the work as a 1999 Oxford University Press publication. Google Books’ author note describes Blackburn as a philosophy professor at Cambridge and records his earlier fellowship and teaching at Pembroke College, Oxford. University College Oxford hosts a student review that discusses the book’s chapters on God, free will, reasoning and knowledge, and notes that a reader may approach chapters selectively. That review is a reader’s account, not an official publisher statement or a substitute for the text itself.
profiles.before_reading: This is an introduction, not a neutral dictionary of every philosophical position. Expect arguments, objections and conceptual distinctions. You do not need to read every chapter in strict order: the Oxford student review describes reading the introduction and then moving to chapters of personal interest. A sequential reading is still useful if you want to see how epistemology, mind, freedom and ethics connect.
profiles.literary_approach: Blackburn organizes the book by problems rather than by a chronological history of philosophers. This can make abstract debates easier to compare, but it also means the author’s choices shape which questions receive emphasis. A productive method is to write down each argument’s premises, conclusion and strongest objection instead of only recording whether you agree.
profiles.context: The work belongs to the tradition of accessible analytic-philosophy introductions. Its 1999 publication date and Oxford University Press imprint are confirmed in bibliographic records. It should be read as a late-twentieth-century introduction, not as a current survey of every contemporary debate in philosophy or cognitive science.

themes.label: Knowledge and skepticism
themes.discussion: What justifies belief, and how far can ordinary confidence survive skeptical questions about appearance and reality?

themes.label: Mind and personal identity
themes.discussion: The chapters on mind and the self invite distinctions between experience, consciousness, bodily continuity and the idea of a person.

themes.label: Freedom and responsibility
themes.discussion: The free-will chapter creates a bridge between metaphysical questions and everyday judgments about choice and accountability.

themes.label: Reasoning about ultimate questions
themes.discussion: The chapters on God, reasoning and what to do provide a place to examine how arguments work across different domains.

profiles.personal_fit: Your philosophy pathway makes this a foundational title: it offers a broad map before narrower works such as Russell’s Problems of Philosophy. Its chapter on reasoning can also provide a vocabulary for evaluating claims and distinguishing a persuasive argument from a confident assertion.
profiles.possible_mismatch: The book is conceptual rather than narrative. If you want a continuous story or a hands-on workbook, it may feel abstract. Its 1999 framing also means later developments in psychology and philosophy will need separate sources rather than being assumed to appear here.

notes: The Oxford student review describes discussion of arguments for and against the existence of God, including classical arguments and the problem of evil.
No exhaustive content or difficulty audit has been performed.

reading_questions: Which assumptions about knowledge do you rely on without noticing?
What is the strongest version of the opposing argument in each chapter?
Does the chapter on free will change how you distinguish explanation from excuse?
discussion_questions: Is a problem easier to understand when it is organized by question rather than historical period?
Which philosophical questions can be investigated with empirical evidence, and which require conceptual argument?

related_connections.label: A second philosophy introduction
related_connections.note: Russell’s earlier work gives a narrower, historically situated treatment of epistemology and metaphysics; this connection is an editorial pairing, not a formal series.

profiles.title: The Righteous Mind
profiles.author: Jonathan Haidt
profiles.verification_scope: Publisher work page, author biography and named Vintage paperback metadata verified. The planned reader edition is not identified.

publication.basis: Author biography identifies The Righteous Mind as a 2012 book; publisher lists 2012 hardcover and 2013 paperback.

profiles.genre_and_form: Popular social psychology and moral psychology. It combines explanatory argument with research examples to explore how people form moral judgments and why moral communities can cooperate internally while disagreeing sharply with outsiders.
profiles.summary: Jonathan Haidt asks why people can be sincere about morality and still arrive at sharply different conclusions. The book presents his account of moral judgment as strongly intuitive, with conscious reasoning often arriving afterward to explain or defend a response. It then considers how moral concerns help people coordinate within groups and why those same group bonds can deepen conflict. The publisher describes the book as drawing on Haidt’s research in moral psychology and comparing moral intuitions across ideological communities. The central invitation is not simply to agree with Haidt, but to understand how moral certainty is formed and what it makes easier—or harder—to see.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Haidt’s official biography identifies him as a social psychologist at New York University and describes his earlier research as examining intuitive foundations of morality and variation across cultural and political divisions. The publisher’s page identifies the hardcover as published in 2012 and a Vintage paperback edition in 2013.
profiles.before_reading: Treat the book’s explanatory framework as a model to examine, not as a final inventory of every person’s moral life. Keep three questions separate: what Haidt reports from research, how he interprets those findings, and what conclusions he draws about public disagreement. The book discusses political and religious differences; the aim of this profile is analysis, not a claim that one group’s moral outlook is inherently superior.
profiles.literary_approach: The book moves between a large explanatory thesis, research-based examples and applications to group life. Its accessible style makes it suitable for discussion, but its broad synthesis can compress complex literatures. When a claim feels especially sweeping, note what kind of evidence would support it and what counterexample might narrow it.
profiles.context: The publisher categorizes the book under psychology, philosophy and politics. Haidt’s biography places the work within his research on moral psychology. This profile does not independently re-evaluate every study discussed in the book; readers should consult original studies and later scholarship before treating any single claim as settled.

themes.label: Intuition and reasoning
themes.discussion: The book foregrounds the possibility that moral judgments begin as intuitions and that reasoning may often serve a justificatory role.

themes.label: Moral pluralism
themes.discussion: Different communities may emphasize different moral concerns; understanding disagreement requires asking what each side believes it is protecting.

themes.label: Group belonging
themes.discussion: The same moral commitments that make cooperation possible can also strengthen boundaries between groups.

themes.label: Humility in disagreement
themes.discussion: A practical question is whether understanding another person’s moral framework changes how you argue, even when it does not change your conclusion.

profiles.personal_fit: This is directly aligned with the nonfiction-research pathway and with your interest in moral reasoning, worldviews, bias and evidence. It can pair well with your philosophy reading because it asks how people actually reach moral judgments, while philosophy asks how those judgments should be assessed.
profiles.possible_mismatch: It is a broad synthesis, not a neutral encyclopedia. If you prefer every empirical claim to be accompanied by a full methodological discussion, some sections may feel compressed. Its political and religious examples may also feel repetitive if you want a narrowly philosophical treatment.

notes: The publisher describes discussion of morality, politics, religion and social division.
No exhaustive content audit or chapter-by-chapter sensitivity review has been performed.

reading_questions: When does a moral intuition arrive before you can explain it?
What evidence would make you revise an interpretation of another group’s values?
Where does the book distinguish describing moral psychology from prescribing moral behavior?
discussion_questions: Can understanding a moral framework reduce hostility without requiring agreement?
What are the limits of using broad group labels to explain individual moral reasoning?

related_connections.label: Self-justification and belief
related_connections.note: Mistakes Were Made examines one mechanism by which people protect a valued self-image after error; the pairing is thematic, not a series.

related_connections.label: Philosophy and reasoning
related_connections.note: Think provides a conceptual companion for evaluating arguments about morality and reason.

profiles.title: The Two Towers
profiles.author: J. R. R. Tolkien
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level position and publication history checked through Tolkien Estate; a 2002 HarperCollins edition record was consulted. No exact reader edition is identified.

publication.basis: The Forodrim chronological bibliography records the first UK publication of The Two Towers on 11 November 1954; Pressmark’s first-edition record independently gives 11 November 1954.

profiles.genre_and_form: Epic fantasy; the middle volume of the continuous narrative commonly published as The Lord of the Rings. The book’s structure follows separated groups of characters rather than one uninterrupted party narrative.

series.name: The Lord of the Rings
series.sequence_status: The Tolkien Estate describes the work as one very large book issued in three volumes for material reasons, rather than a story originally conceived as a trilogy.

profiles.summary: The second volume continues after the Fellowship has been broken apart. Its narrative follows different groups across Middle-earth: some companions pursue the captured hobbits and become entangled in the fate of Rohan and the forest of Fangorn, while Frodo and Sam continue their dangerous journey with Gollum as guide. The split structure gives the reader contrasting forms of struggle—open conflict and political consequence on one side, secrecy, endurance and the psychological pressure of the Ring on the other. The volume expands the world while making the cost of separation increasingly visible.
profiles.author_and_work_background: The Tolkien Estate describes The Lord of the Rings as a work that grew over seventeen years and explains that it was published in three volumes because of material constraints. A specialist chronological bibliography and a first-edition bibliographic record date The Two Towers to 11 November 1954. The Estate page’s broad statement that the later volumes appeared in 1955 conflicts with those volume-specific records; this profile uses the title-specific 1954 date and retains that discrepancy rather than silently smoothing it over.
profiles.before_reading: This is the middle installment of one continuous narrative. The protected reading plan places The Two Towers before The Return of the King, and it is best approached after The Fellowship of the Ring rather than as an independent starting point. The divided narrative is deliberate: remember which characters know what, and notice how distance changes what each group can understand.
profiles.literary_approach: Tolkien alternates narrative strands and scales: intimate travel, shifting alliances, landscape, military movement and the slow passage of the Ring-bearers. The Estate’s account of his maps and chronological revisions is useful background for noticing how geography shapes suspense. The book’s title has a deliberately layered referent; do not assume the phrase has only one obvious interpretation.
profiles.context: The Tolkien Estate notes that the work emerged from a requested sequel to The Hobbit and grew into a much larger history connected to Tolkien’s wider invented world. The Estate also documents the extensive drafting and mapping process. These are authorial-context facts; claims that the novel is a direct allegory for a particular war or political event should not be treated as established without further evidence.

themes.label: Loyalty under separation
themes.discussion: The narrative asks what loyalty looks like when companions cannot remain together or share the same information.

themes.label: Power and temptation
themes.discussion: The Ring’s pressure is not only an external danger; it complicates trust, judgment and endurance.

themes.label: Nature and industrial power
themes.discussion: The contrast between living landscapes and destructive forces invites ecological interpretation, but should be grounded in scenes rather than reduced to a single allegory.

themes.label: Mercy and moral consequence
themes.discussion: The story makes room for the possibility that an earlier act of restraint can shape later events.

profiles.personal_fit: This is a major planned fantasy-arc installment, with detailed worldbuilding, multiple narrative threads and a sustained moral struggle. It may reward the kind of close, reflective reading that tracks how character choices and institutional power affect one another across a large story.
profiles.possible_mismatch: The prose and pacing are deliberately expansive, and the book is not a fast, single-viewpoint adventure. If you want every chapter to stay with one character group, the structural division may feel abrupt until the two strands are considered together.

notes: Publisher and estate materials describe war, pursuit, peril and the Ring-bearers’ dangerous journey.
This is an epic-fantasy conflict narrative; no exhaustive content-warning audit has been performed.

reading_questions: How does the split structure alter your sense of urgency?
Which characters act with incomplete information, and how does that affect your judgment of them?
What does the landscape make possible or impossible for each group?
discussion_questions: Is the Ring primarily a symbol of power, addiction, domination, or something more complicated?
How does the novel distinguish mercy from weakness?

related_connections.note: The Return of the King is the third volume and continues the same continuous narrative.

profiles.title: The Sword of Kaigen
profiles.author: M. L. Wang
profiles.verification_scope: Author’s official book page and an author interview indexed by NYU’s Greene Street Review were consulted. Standalone status and author-described genre/context are verified; exact edition, page count and audio duration are not.

publication.basis: The author’s official page describes the work and its place relative to Theonite books; bibliographic search records identify the 2019 release. Exact reader edition remains unknown.

profiles.genre_and_form: Military fantasy, martial-arts fantasy and family drama, using elemental magic in a fictional empire. The author calls it a standalone novel even though it is set earlier than two works in the wider Theonite universe.

series.name: Theonite universe (shared setting)
series.sequence_status: The author explicitly describes The Sword of Kaigen as a standalone novel set thirteen years before Planet Adyn and Orbit. It does not require reading those books first.

profiles.summary: On the Kusanagi Peninsula, the Matsuda family belongs to a society that prizes formidable elemental warriors and has built its identity around defending the Kaigenese Empire. Mamoru, a teenager raised to inherit that martial duty, begins to question the official story of peace after an outsider reveals troubling information. His mother Misaki has a different history: she once fought, but marriage and family life have pushed that identity into the background. As threats approach from beyond the peninsula, the family’s private tensions and the empire’s public story begin to collide.
profiles.author_and_work_background: M. L. Wang’s official page labels the novel military fantasy and foregrounds the Matsuda family, their martial training and the empire’s public story of peace. It takes place thirteen years before Planet Adyn and Orbit while remaining readable as a standalone. The author also explains that the story began as a serialized newsletter project before expanding into a full novel. An NYU Greene Street Review interview provides additional author commentary on propaganda, abuses of power and the writer’s background in history and martial-arts training; the page was available in search indexing but could not be fully opened during this research pass, so those interview details are supplementary rather than essential profile claims.
profiles.before_reading: The book is not a simple martial-arts adventure. The official author description emphasizes both Mamoru’s inherited duty and Misaki’s suppressed past, and it explicitly identifies family drama alongside military fantasy. The author recommends the book for readers sixteen and older, noting that it treats more difficult themes and subject matter than the younger-skewing Theonite books. The author’s standalone note means you do not need to read the related Theonite novels first.
profiles.literary_approach: The central contrast is between a public story of national strength and the private costs carried by people expected to sustain it. Alternating attention between a younger character and an adult mother gives the family conflict more than one generational perspective. The author’s stated genre labels support the military-fantasy and family-drama framing; interpretations about propaganda and inherited duty are developed from the official synopsis and author commentary.
profiles.context: The author describes a fictional Kaigenese Empire, the Kusanagi Peninsula, elemental powers and a martial-fantasy setting. These are elements of the novel’s invented world; the profile does not equate the fictional society with any single real country or culture. The author interview indexed by NYU includes a discussion of propaganda and power, but the full page could not be opened during this research pass, so those interview details are supplementary rather than essential profile claims.

themes.label: Inherited duty and chosen identity
themes.discussion: Mamoru’s training and Misaki’s buried martial past offer contrasting ways a family can shape, constrain and transmit identity.

themes.label: Official stories and propaganda
themes.discussion: The novel’s premise asks how a society maintains a narrative of peace and strength when evidence begins to contradict it.

themes.label: Family as both refuge and pressure
themes.discussion: The Matsuda household is not separate from the political conflict; family relationships are one of the places where public expectations become intimate.

themes.label: Skill, violence and responsibility
themes.discussion: Martial competence may protect people, but it also raises questions about what violence can and cannot repair.

profiles.personal_fit: The novel intersects with your interests in family, identity, institutions, inherited expectations and the difference between a public belief system and the people who live under it. Its standalone structure makes it easy to approach without adding a new unfinished series obligation.
profiles.possible_mismatch: The author explicitly recommends it for readers sixteen and older and describes more difficult themes. The military-fantasy setting includes conflict and intense family material; if you want a lighter fantasy between nonfiction titles, this may not serve as a restful palate cleanser.

notes: The author recommends readers be at least sixteen and describes the book as dealing with more difficult themes and subject matter.
The official synopsis includes impending invasion, military conflict, family strain and the threat of violence.
This is not an exhaustive content-warning audit.

reading_questions: Who benefits from the official story of peace, and who is asked to maintain it?
How do Mamoru and Misaki understand duty differently?
What does the family protect, and what does it conceal?
discussion_questions: Can a person remain loyal to a community while rejecting the story that community tells about itself?
How does the novel distinguish inherited skill from inherited obligation?

related_connections.label: Another standalone epic fantasy
related_connections.note: The Spear Cuts Through Water also places intimate relationships inside a wider conflict over power; this is a thematic pairing, not a shared series.

profiles.title: A Hat Full of Sky
profiles.author: Terry Pratchett
profiles.verification_scope: Official author page verifies publication date, synopsis and Tiffany Aching context. Exact reader edition and audiobook have not been identified.
profiles.genre_and_form: Comic fantasy and the second Tiffany Aching novel within Discworld. It follows the opening novel, The Wee Free Men, and develops Tiffany’s apprenticeship as a witch.

series.name: Tiffany Aching / Discworld
series.sequence_status: The author’s official Tiffany Aching materials list the five-book sequence.

profiles.summary: Tiffany is now eleven and begins the work of learning witchcraft under the guidance of Miss Level, with the formidable Granny Weatherwax also part of the story’s circle of witches. The apprenticeship is not the effortless collection of spells she may have imagined: it involves ordinary work, responsibility and learning what a witch is for. A dangerous, disembodied presence is drawn toward Tiffany after an unusual experience leaves her vulnerable. The novel combines the comic texture of Discworld with a more intimate question about identity: what makes a person themselves, and what happens when that boundary is threatened?
profiles.author_and_work_background: The official Terry Pratchett site gives the publication date as 29 April 2004. The author’s chronology also records the 2005 Locus Award for Best Young Adult Book for A Hat Full of Sky. The official Tiffany Aching category places it after The Wee Free Men and before Wintersmith.
profiles.before_reading: This is the second Tiffany Aching book. The official synopsis identifies Tiffany as eleven, ready for witch training, and learning alongside Miss Level and Granny Weatherwax. Reading The Wee Free Men first will preserve the character’s progression and the reader’s understanding of the Chalk and the Nac Mac Feegle, though the official site’s synopsis does not state that prior reading is mandatory.
profiles.literary_approach: The apprenticeship structure gives the book a way to distinguish appearance from practice: a role may look glamorous from outside, while its real value lies in attention, labor and service. The supernatural threat externalizes a question of personal boundaries. This is an interpretive reading of the official setup, not a claim that the author supplied one definitive allegory.
profiles.context: The book sits in a sequence that follows Tiffany as she grows older. The official author materials give a rough progression of ages across the five books and identify the Chalk as her home. The profile treats witchcraft as a fictional social role and does not present the novel as a historical account of real witch traditions.

themes.label: Apprenticeship and responsibility
themes.discussion: Learning a role means accepting its ordinary duties, not only acquiring the abilities that look exciting.

themes.label: Selfhood and bodily boundaries
themes.discussion: The official synopsis describes Tiffany leaving her body and becoming vulnerable to an ancient presence; this invites careful questions about agency and identity.

themes.label: Mentorship without imitation
themes.discussion: Tiffany learns from older witches whose methods and personalities differ; apprenticeship need not mean becoming a copy of a mentor.

themes.label: Humility and practical work
themes.discussion: The gap between imagined magic and daily chores gives the book a comic route into the ethics of useful work.

profiles.personal_fit: This continues a planned series arc and adds a stronger mentorship and selfhood dimension to the first Tiffany book. It is a natural companion to your interest in capable characters, identity, responsibility and the way values become visible through everyday actions.
profiles.possible_mismatch: The threat is more psychological and bodily than a simple external monster, and the story includes apprenticeship chores alongside fantasy action. Readers wanting nonstop action may find the deliberate learning process slower.

notes: The official synopsis describes an episode in which Tiffany leaves her body and an ancient, dangerous presence seeks a body to inhabit.
The book includes frightening supernatural threat and vulnerability of bodily autonomy.
This is not an exhaustive content-warning audit.

reading_questions: What is the difference between wanting a title and accepting the work it requires?
How do the different witches model different kinds of authority?
What does the story suggest makes a person recognizably themselves?
discussion_questions: Can mentorship help someone become more themselves rather than more like the mentor?
How does humor change the way the book handles bodily vulnerability and fear?

profiles.title: Mistakes Were Made (But Not by Me)
profiles.author: Carol Tavris and Elliot Aronson
profiles.verification_scope: Third-edition bibliographic metadata and subject scope checked through Google Books and Social Psychology Network; author qualifications cross-checked against publisher pages. Reader edition remains unknown.

publication.basis: The source records identify the 2020 third revised edition; first-edition year is not used for reader-edition metadata.

profiles.genre_and_form: Popular social psychology. The third edition applies cognitive-dissonance theory to self-justification across personal, institutional and public contexts, using research and illustrative cases.

series.sequence_status: Standalone nonfiction work co-authored by Carol Tavris and Elliot Aronson.

profiles.summary: Tavris and Aronson examine why admitting a mistake can feel so difficult even when the evidence is clear. Their central subject is self-justification: the mental work people do to protect a valued picture of themselves as reasonable, decent or correct. The book applies cognitive-dissonance theory to a wide range of settings, including personal relationships, memory, law, business and political conflict. Its usefulness lies in making a familiar human habit visible: once a person has invested in a decision or identity, new information may be treated as a threat to manage rather than evidence to consider.
profiles.author_and_work_background: The third revised edition was published in 2020. Social Psychology Network’s profile of Carol Tavris identifies her as a social psychologist and notes that the third edition added a chapter on dissonance, democracy and demagoguery. Macmillan’s author page describes Elliot Aronson as a social psychologist and lists this book among his works. The bibliographic record consulted lists 466 pages for the Pinter & Martin edition, while other catalogues report 464; that discrepancy is retained rather than concealed.
profiles.before_reading: The title is pointed, but the book’s subject is not limited to obviously foolish people. The authors examine how ordinary people, professionals and institutions can rationalize actions after committing to them. Read examples critically: distinguish the psychological mechanism being discussed from the authors’ interpretation of any particular case, and look for the evidence that supports each application.
profiles.literary_approach: The authors combine an explanatory psychological concept with case-based examples. This makes abstract theory concrete, but examples are not a substitute for representative data. A useful reading practice is to mark each passage as theory, research finding, case illustration or interpretation. That separation helps prevent the book’s vivid examples from being mistaken for proof of how frequently a behavior occurs.
profiles.context: Cognitive dissonance is associated with Leon Festinger’s work; the title page of the third edition dedicates the book to him. Tavris and Aronson apply the theory to modern social and institutional questions. The profile does not independently audit each study or legal case discussed in the book.

themes.label: Self-justification
themes.discussion: A person may protect their self-image by changing the story about an action rather than reconsidering the action itself.

themes.label: Evidence and identity
themes.discussion: New evidence can feel like a threat to belonging, competence or moral identity; that pressure may affect how it is evaluated.

themes.label: Institutional accountability
themes.discussion: The book’s scope invites examination of how professional systems can preserve error when many people have incentives to defend prior decisions.

themes.label: Repair after error
themes.discussion: The possibility of acknowledging a mistake raises questions about apology, restitution and whether changed behavior is more important than a revised self-description.

profiles.personal_fit: This is an especially useful research-pathway companion to The Righteous Mind and your interests in cognitive biases, misinformation, ethics and institutional responsibility. It offers a precise vocabulary for distinguishing genuine change from a narrative that only produces a feeling of absolution.
profiles.possible_mismatch: The subject matter can be uncomfortable because the examples implicate everyday relationships as well as public institutions. The book’s case-driven style may also feel repetitive if you prefer a tightly formal philosophical argument.

notes: The author profile lists discussion of memory, criminal justice, police interrogation, family quarrels, political polarization and conflicts of interest.
These topics may include distressing case examples. The list is not exhaustive and does not establish how much detail appears in any given edition.

reading_questions: When does a person update a belief, and when do they update the explanation for holding it?
What evidence would distinguish a sincere correction from a self-protective narrative?
How do institutions distribute responsibility when a harmful decision has many contributors?
discussion_questions: Can self-justification ever protect a person from unproductive shame, and when does it become an obstacle to repair?
What would a meaningful accountability process need to preserve evidence and allow correction?

related_connections.note: The Righteous Mind considers intuition and group morality; this book focuses on dissonance and self-justification. The pairing is thematic.

related_connections.note: Think supplies a philosophy-oriented companion for evaluating arguments and standards of justification.

profiles.title: The Problems of Philosophy
profiles.author: Bertrand Russell
profiles.verification_scope: Original 1912 publication, chapter structure and broad intellectual context verified through Project Gutenberg, Google Books and Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Modern edition and translation not identified.

publication.basis: Project Gutenberg and Google Books identify the original H. Holt 1912 publication.

profiles.genre_and_form: A concise philosophical introduction, organized as fifteen chapters that move through appearance and reality, matter, idealism, knowledge, induction, universals, truth, error and the value of philosophy.

series.sequence_status: Standalone classic work; no series placement identified.

profiles.summary: Russell begins with a familiar object—the table—and asks whether its appearance tells us what it is really like. From that simple puzzle, the book opens into questions about the external world, perception, matter and how knowledge can be justified. It then moves through induction, general principles, universals, truth, error and the limits of philosophical knowledge. Rather than promising final answers to every problem, Russell presents philosophy as a disciplined examination of questions that ordinary confidence can hide. The final chapter asks what value philosophy has if it cannot settle every dispute.
profiles.author_and_work_background: The original book was published in 1912 as part of the Home University Library of Modern Knowledge. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy identifies Russell as a British philosopher, logician, essayist and social critic, and places him among the founders of modern analytic philosophy alongside G. E. Moore. His broader work includes mathematical logic, epistemology, ethics and public writing.
profiles.before_reading: The text is more than a century old. Some examples and terminology reflect the philosophical debates of its time, so use it as a historical argument, not a complete map of current epistemology or metaphysics. The chapter sequence is useful for building a conceptual spine: perception, knowledge, induction and truth lead toward the question of what philosophy can reasonably claim.
profiles.literary_approach: Russell often starts from an everyday puzzle and uses it to introduce a distinction or argument. The method is analytic: identify what is being claimed, ask what the evidence can support, and separate immediate experience from assumptions about what exists beyond it. The book’s clarity is part of its persuasive force, but clarity should not be confused with the absence of contestable premises.
profiles.context: The work appeared in 1912, during Russell’s early analytic-philosophy period. The Stanford Encyclopedia entry provides a broader account of his work in logic and philosophy, while the book itself is a popular introduction rather than a technical research monograph. The original H. Holt catalogue record lists 255 pages; later editions may be shorter or longer.

themes.label: Appearance and reality
themes.discussion: How much can perception tell us about an object independent of the conditions under which we perceive it?

themes.label: Knowledge and justification
themes.discussion: The distinction between knowing something directly and knowing it through description creates a framework for asking what a claim rests on.

themes.label: Induction and general principles
themes.discussion: The book asks how experience can justify expectations that go beyond the cases already observed.

themes.label: The value of inquiry
themes.discussion: The closing chapter considers whether clarifying questions and widening possibilities has value even without final certainty.

profiles.personal_fit: This is a strong companion to Think, but it offers a more historically situated and tightly epistemological route into philosophy. It fits your interest in distinguishing what is known, what is inferred and what is merely asserted—especially useful when researching contested claims or evaluating confident explanations.
profiles.possible_mismatch: The language and examples belong to an earlier philosophical moment. Some arguments may feel dated, and the work is abstract rather than narrative. It should be paired with newer sources if you want to understand contemporary positions.

notes: This is a philosophical argument rather than a narrative work.
It discusses religious and metaphysical questions, including idealism and the limits of knowledge.
No exhaustive difficulty or content audit has been performed.

reading_questions: What does the table example show about the gap between perception and reality?
Which premises does Russell need for an argument about induction?
What kind of uncertainty does he regard as productive rather than defeating?
discussion_questions: Does a philosophical problem become less important if it cannot be conclusively solved?
How would a contemporary cognitive scientist respond to Russell’s account of perception and knowledge?

related_connections.note: Think provides a later, broader introduction to philosophy; this is an editorial pairing rather than a formal sequence.

profiles.title: The Return of the King
profiles.author: J. R. R. Tolkien
profiles.verification_scope: Tolkien Estate work history and Google Books title-level edition records verified. Exact reader edition, pagination and appendices configuration remain unknown.

publication.basis: The Forodrim chronological bibliography records first UK publication on 20 October 1955; the Tolkien Estate also dates this volume to 1955.

profiles.genre_and_form: Epic fantasy; the third volume of The Lord of the Rings, which the Tolkien Estate describes as one continuous work published in three volumes for material reasons.

series.name: The Lord of the Rings
series.sequence_status: Final volume of the continuous narrative; the estate cautions against treating the three physical volumes as a trilogy originally conceived as three independent stories.

profiles.summary: The final volume brings the scattered movements of the Ring-bearers and the wider conflict toward their decisive point. The forces of Sauron gather, while Aragorn’s claim and responsibilities become increasingly public and Frodo and Sam continue toward the heart of Mordor. The volume moves between military and political events, intimate acts of endurance and the question of what victory can mean after prolonged loss. Its conclusion is not only about whether a quest succeeds; it also asks what a restored world owes to those who carried the cost of its survival.
profiles.author_and_work_background: The Tolkien Estate dates The Return of the King to 1955 and describes the full work as the product of seventeen years of composition. Its account explains that the three-volume publication was a material decision prompted by the book’s size, not evidence that Tolkien initially conceived three separate novels. The Estate also discusses Tolkien’s maps, appendices and careful management of chronology.
profiles.before_reading: This is the final volume and should follow The Fellowship of the Ring and The Two Towers. The work includes more than the central quest: the Tolkien Estate highlights appendices, languages, histories and genealogies as material Tolkien considered important even when they might slow the main narrative. The edition you choose may include different appendices, maps or illustrations, so page counts can vary dramatically.
profiles.literary_approach: The final volume has to resolve several narrative scales at once: the fate of the Ring, the political future of kingdoms, and the personal consequences of a long journey. The Estate’s account of Tolkien’s chronology and appendices helps explain why the world feels historical beyond the immediate plot. A useful lens is the difference between public restoration and private recovery.
profiles.context: Tolkien’s own framing of the work emphasizes its growth into a history with layers of earlier events. The Estate notes that the appendices preserve annals, languages and genealogies, and that the book’s production involved extensive maps and revisions. Interpretations that reduce the work to a single historical allegory should be treated cautiously; the Estate describes a range of conflicting readings.

themes.label: Restoration and responsibility
themes.discussion: The return of political order raises questions about what just leadership requires after violence and upheaval.

themes.label: Endurance and limits
themes.discussion: The quest tests what individuals can continue to carry, and what they cannot simply recover afterward.

themes.label: Power and relinquishment
themes.discussion: The Ring’s power makes victory inseparable from the need to refuse domination.

themes.label: Homecoming and change
themes.discussion: A return to familiar places does not necessarily restore the people who left them to their former selves.

profiles.personal_fit: This completes a major protected fantasy arc and rewards close attention to worldbuilding, political responsibility and character consequences. It also provides a substantial conclusion to questions about power, sacrifice and the difference between winning a conflict and repairing what conflict has damaged.
profiles.possible_mismatch: The ending is expansive and includes material beyond the main narrative in many editions. If you expect a short final sprint, the appendices and edition-dependent extras can make the reading commitment considerably larger.

notes: The publisher and estate materials describe war, armies, peril and the final stages of a dangerous quest.
The volume contains conflict and loss; this is not an exhaustive content-warning audit.

reading_questions: What kind of restoration is possible after a long conflict?
How do private acts of endurance connect to public political change?
What does the work ask its heroes to relinquish?
discussion_questions: Does the ending define victory as the defeat of an enemy, the restoration of a community, or something more complicated?
Why might Tolkien have considered languages, genealogies and annals essential to the work’s meaning?

related_connections.note: The Two Towers is the second volume; this title completes the planned Lord of the Rings sequence.

profiles.title: The Spear Cuts Through Water
profiles.author: Simon Jimenez
profiles.verification_scope: Publisher page, author profile and Kirkus review checked for synopsis, author background, awards, narrative form and specific 2022/2023 edition metadata. The planned reader edition remains unknown.

publication.basis: Penguin Random House lists ebook and audiobook formats in 2022 and paperback publication in 2023.

profiles.genre_and_form: Epic fantasy with a mythic, folktale-inflected frame. Kirkus describes shifts among first-, second- and third-person narration and a dreamlike theatrical frame; the publisher identifies it as an epic fantasy and lists major genre awards.

series.sequence_status: Standalone novel; no series placement is identified by the publisher page.

profiles.summary: Two warriors, Jun and Keema, help an ancient god escape the royal family that has kept her imprisoned beneath its palace. Their journey across a broken land becomes a challenge to the Moon Throne’s rule and a search for a different future. The publisher’s synopsis frames the novel as both a large-scale fantasy about tyranny and a more intimate story about identity, legacy and belonging. Kirkus describes a layered narrative in which a present-day listener enters a dreamlike theater and experiences a tale through changing narrative perspectives. The result asks the reader to consider not only what a story says, but who is telling it and how it is remembered.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Penguin Random House identifies The Spear Cuts Through Water as Simon Jimenez’s second book after The Vanished Birds. Its product page records a 2022 ebook/audiobook release and a 2023 paperback edition. The publisher lists the novel as winner of the IAFA Crawford Award and British Fantasy Award, and as shortlisted for the Ursula K. Le Guin and Ignyte awards. The author profile describes Jimenez’s short fiction and MFA study at Emerson College.
profiles.before_reading: The narrative form is part of the experience. Kirkus describes the story as moving among first, second and third person, with a framing device involving a dreamlike theater and remembered tales. Expect the reader’s position to shift; the second-person address is not merely a decorative trick. The book also includes violence and political oppression, so it is not a gentle folktale despite its mythic structure.
profiles.literary_approach: The frame narrative makes storytelling visible: a tale is remembered, performed, inhabited and passed on. The shifts in grammatical person can make the reader feel both outside and inside the action. This technique invites questions about inheritance, cultural memory and the relationship between individual experience and shared legend. These are interpretive observations grounded in the form described by Kirkus, not a claim that every reader will experience the device in the same way.
profiles.context: The publisher and Kirkus describe a fantasy world under a long-running royal order, with an ancient god held beneath the palace and a journey that challenges the existing regime. The publisher lists awards and nominations, which establish the book’s reception history but do not determine its quality for an individual reader.

themes.label: Storytelling as inheritance
themes.discussion: The frame narrative connects memory, family transmission and the way stories become part of a person’s sense of home.

themes.label: Power and liberation
themes.discussion: The journey challenges a royal order that sustains itself through coercion and the exploitation of a divine source of power.

themes.label: Identity and belonging
themes.discussion: The publisher explicitly identifies identity, legacy and belonging among the novel’s central concerns.

themes.label: Form and participation
themes.discussion: The changing narrative person can make the reader feel implicated in the act of receiving and retelling a story.

profiles.personal_fit: This could be an especially rewarding choice if you enjoy ambitious prose, layered storytelling, mythology, family memory and political questions embedded in fantasy. It offers a distinct contrast to the more conventional quest structure of Tolkien and the more domestic military-fantasy focus of The Sword of Kaigen.
profiles.possible_mismatch: The narrative frame and shifting point of view may require sustained attention. The publisher and reviewers describe violence and an oppressive regime; if you want a straightforward, linear adventure, the formal experimentation may be demanding.

notes: The publisher synopsis describes tyranny, imprisonment, oppression and a dangerous journey.
Kirkus describes the book as involving bloody conflict and depicts a character’s PTSD and disability as part of the narrative.
This is not an exhaustive content-warning audit; the publisher and reviewer summaries do not replace a full-text content review.

reading_questions: Who is speaking at each point, and what changes when the narrative addresses “you”?
How does the frame story alter the meaning of the central journey?
What is the difference between defeating a ruler and undoing the system that sustains the ruler?
discussion_questions: Can a story preserve a community’s memory while also changing it?
How does the novel use form to make the reader a participant rather than a distant observer?
